blocks.title: Gobu: a local abuse becomes a challenge to authority
paragraphs: The 1894 crisis began with rural grievances in and around Gobu, where the conduct of local official Jo Byeong-gap became a focus of anger. Allegations about taxation, imposed work and abusive administration were not abstract complaints against modernization. They concerned the way households experienced state officials, levies and uncertainty about justice. Jeon Bong-jun's organizing drew energy from this concrete conflict, but the movement soon extended beyond one magistrate.

The episode shows how a local grievance could become a test of broader political legitimacy. The removal or replacement of an official did not necessarily satisfy farmers who had discovered the possibility of collective action. The movement also inherited networks shaped by Donghak religion and earlier petitions, making it capable of reaching beyond a single county. Historians should distinguish the immediate Gobu protest from the subsequent regional mobilization rather than treating the entire year as one continuous army under one unchanging command.

blocks.title: Leadership and the Donghak connection
paragraphs: Jeon Bong-jun was a leading organizer, but rural protest involved many local figures, religious leaders, village networks and participants whose motives differed. Some were committed Donghak adherents; others responded to unfair taxation or the abuse of political power. Donghak supplied organizational links, moral language and opportunities for trust across communities. Its religious character was not merely a disguise for economic rebellion.

The movement's strength depended partly on the ability to gather people and provisions while operating in a territory crossed by official forces. Participants had to communicate rapidly, assess risks and coordinate when to fight or negotiate. Official reports tend to describe leaders and enemies, while later commemorative accounts can magnify individual heroism. A historically responsible narrative uses named leaders without erasing the collective and locally rooted nature of the uprising.

blocks.title: Hwangtohyeon and the credibility of armed protest
paragraphs: The peasant army's victories, including the battle of Hwangtohyeon, altered the government's calculation. An assembly that could defeat official troops was no longer a problem that one local reprimand would settle. The military successes helped strengthen recruitment and confidence among supporters while increasing anxiety in the central court and among local elites.

Winning a battle did not solve the movement's practical challenges. Volunteers needed food, shelter, effective communications and means of preventing disorder in areas they passed through. Military success could also attract participants with different expectations of reform. The peasant leadership had to manage an unstable coalition whose grievances ranged from abusive officials to wider questions of status, public revenue and outside influence. Sources that describe victories in heroic shorthand can obscure this organizational work.

blocks.title: Jeonju and the paradox of success
paragraphs: The occupation of Jeonju, the provincial centre, represented a major escalation because it challenged a key administrative node. The government confronted the difficulty of suppressing an organized force while imperial neighbors were already attentive to Korea's internal affairs. A local movement was becoming a regional political crisis with international consequences.

The capture of the city did not mean that peasant forces could immediately govern the entire kingdom or replace the central monarchy. Their bargaining power depended on conditions in Jeolla and on the ability of official forces to recover control. The distinction matters because later nationalist accounts may retroactively read a comprehensive revolution into every action, while hostile official narratives sometimes reduce political demands to violence. The evidence points to an active contest over administration and reform.

blocks.title: Jeonju agreement and temporary accommodation
paragraphs: The arrangement usually termed the Jeonju agreement or Jeonju Hwayak followed the military and political confrontation. Accounts differ in how precisely they describe its terms and the formal status of commitments. It provided an opening for withdrawal and for local forms of reform activity, rather than settling all disputes between the movement and the government.

The peasant army's subsequent establishment of jipgangso offices in Jeolla demonstrates that participants sought more than battlefield success. They attempted to supervise local administration and address everyday abuses. Yet the extent of effective control varied by town, and these bodies coexisted uneasily with official institutions. One should not imagine a single centrally codified democratic constitution operating uniformly across the province; the evidence instead shows uneven experiments in political participation.

blocks.title: A Korean struggle with foreign consequences
paragraphs: The government's appeal to Qing forces and Japan's dispatch of troops transformed the setting in which the peasant movement operated. Korean reform demands became entangled with a rivalry between empires. Contemporary diplomatic records show Korean officials protesting the continued presence of foreign troops after the immediate justification for intervention had changed.

The international consequence should not erase the movement's own agenda. Farmers did not organize simply to provide a pretext for a Sino-Japanese war. They challenged abuses and debated the kind of government that could protect livelihoods and dignity. The following unit owns the diplomatic and military escalation between Qing and Japan, while the peasant story retains its independent chronology and substantive demands.
